chunks: It seems as if you do not want (to please) Allāh by your jihād,
and as if you do not stand upon a clear sign from your Lord,
and as if you have been playing tricks with this ummah (Muslim community) to earn (the pleasure of) this world
and watching for the moment of their neglectfulness to usurp their share of the wealth.
As soon as it was possible for you to misappropriate the ummah’s trust,
you hastened to turn around and attack (them),
and made a swift leap to snatch away whatever you could from their property meant for their widows and their orphans
as a wolf snatches a wounded and helpless goat.
Then, you happily loaded it off to the Ḥijāz
without feeling guilty for having appropriated it.
Allāh’s woe be to your ill-wishers; it was as though you were sending to your family what you had inherited from your father and mother.

key_terms.جِهَادُ: striving or exertion, often referring to military or spiritual struggle in this context
key_terms.حِجَازٌ: a region in western Arabia including Mecca and Medina
key_terms.فَيْءٌ: booty or wealth acquired without fighting

ai.seo_question: How does Imam Ali criticize the misuse of public funds for personal gain?
ai.summary: This passage from Nahj al-Balagha criticizes an officer for prioritizing worldly gain over divine pleasure, accusing him of exploiting the community's trust to seize wealth designated for widows and orphans. It uses vivid imagery of a wolf snatching a goat to describe his swift and greedy appropriation of these funds, which he then transported to the Hijaz with pride and without remorse. In Shia scholarly tradition, this critique underscores the concept of *ghulul* (misappropriation of war booty) and serves as a moral warning against the corruption of religious duty by material ambition.
